title: Xi Jinping Expected in India for BRICS Summit, First Visit Since Galwan Crisis
excerpt: Wang Yi's New Delhi trip this week signals Beijing has cleared the way for the Chinese president to attend the September summit, capping a diplomatic reset that began in Kazan.
body:
• Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit India for the BRICS Summit in September 2026, marking his first trip to the country since the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley clash
  • Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited New Delhi this week to finalize logistics, signaling Beijing has given the green light for Xi's attendance
  • Prime Minister Modi personally invited Xi during their meeting at the SCO Summit in Tianjin in August 2025, after the two leaders agreed to resume high-level engagement
  • The visit would cap a diplomatic reset that began with the Kazan bilateral in October 2024 and continued through border disengagement agreements

A Visit Six Years in the Making

Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to travel to India for the BRICS Summit scheduled for September 12-13 in New Delhi, according to diplomatic sources familiar with the planning. The visit would be Xi's first to India since October 2019, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi for an informal summit in Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu, just months before the relationship cratered over a deadly border clash in the Galwan Valley.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visit to New Delhi this week is being read by both Indian and international observers as confirmation that Beijing has cleared the way for Xi's attendance. Wang met with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and National Security Advisor Ajit Doval, with discussions covering BRICS Summit logistics, bilateral trade, and the broader framework of the relationship.

Modi personally invited Xi during their bilateral meeting at the SCO Summit in Tianjin in August 2025, after the two leaders agreed to resume high-level engagement following years of frozen ties.

The Long Road From Galwan

The June 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat along the Line of Actual Control, sent India-China relations to their lowest point in decades. India banned over 300 Chinese apps including TikTok and PUBG Mobile, restricted Chinese investment, and deployed tens of thousands of additional troops along the disputed border.

The thaw began cautiously. A breakthrough came at the BRICS Summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024, where Modi and Xi held their first structured bilateral in five years. That meeting produced a border disengagement agreement, with both sides pulling back troops from key friction points in eastern Ladakh. Subsequent meetings at the SCO in Tianjin and the G20 in Johannesburg built incrementally on Kazan.

What Is on the Table

The BRICS Summit agenda extends well beyond the bilateral. India, as the rotating chair, is expected to push for expansion of the New Development Bank's lending capacity, a digital payments interoperability framework among BRICS nations, and coordinated positions on WTO reform. But the Xi-Modi bilateral on the sidelines will inevitably dominate coverage.

Trade between the two countries has continued to grow despite political tensions, reaching 36 billion in 2025 according to Chinese customs data. India's trade deficit with China widened to over 9 billion, a sore point that New Delhi has raised repeatedly. Indian officials are expected to press for greater market access for Indian IT services and pharmaceutical exports, while Beijing is likely to seek relaxation of restrictions on Chinese telecom equipment and FDI screening rules.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the visit carries significance beyond geopolitics. The Galwan crisis reshaped how many NRIs viewed China, accelerating support for supply chain diversification and fueling interest in India as a manufacturing alternative. A successful summit could ease tensions that have rippled into business and academic exchanges, including visa restrictions that have limited people-to-people contact since 2020.

Diplomatic observers caution that the visit, while symbolically important, is unlikely to resolve the underlying border dispute, which involves competing territorial claims across thousands of kilometers of undefined frontier. But the fact that Xi is willing to visit India on Modi's invitation suggests both sides have concluded that managed competition serves their interests better than the frozen hostility of the past six years.
